newsitem.title: SYRIA: Syria, Lebanon sign deals to encourage investment.
newsitem.headline: Syria, Lebanon sign deals to encourage investment.

text.p: Syria and Lebanon on Sunday signed two agreements aimed at encouraging private investment and preventing double taxation.

The deals were signed at the end of talks in Damascus between Syrian Prime Minister Mahmoud Zu'bi and his Lebanese counterpart Rafik al-Hariri, who co-chaired meetings of the joint higher coordination commission.
Hariri told reporters at the end of the talks he was happy with the outcome of the meetings, adding the agrements would help promote economic cooperation between the two states.
But the Lebanese premier said it was too early to talk about achieving economic unity between Syria and Lebanon due to the difference in the economic systems in both states.
Lebanon has a free market economy while Syria, which followed a Socialist system for years, started to liberalise its economy only five years ago.

Officials said a third agreement on setting up joint customs border points was also signed at the end of the talks in which Lebanese and Syrian ministers of finance, economy, transport, agriculture, industry and planning took part.
Both sides also discussed ways of promoting trade between Syria and Lebanon and how to offset the deficit in the balance of trade which favours Syria.
They said the value of Lebanon's imports from Syria stood at $240 million while Syria's imports from Lebanon according to official data did not exceed $70 million.

But economic sources said Syria's imports from Lebanon included hundreds of millions of dollars handled by smugglers benefiting from low customs duties in Lebanon to smuggle cheap goods to Syria. These imports did not show in official data.

According to the investment deal, both sides would "work to create the appropriate climate to encourage investors and businessmen to set up industrial, agricultural, tourism, and other projects which would contribute in the economic development in both states."

The deal also calls for the protection of private investment in both states and to give investors incentives including tax-free operations for long periods that would be defined in special decrees to be issued by both states.

Syria, the main foreign power broker in Lebanon where it has some 35,000 troops, signed a friendship and cooperation accord with Lebanon in 1991 calling for cooperation in all fields including military, security and politics.
Lebanese officials said political and security cooperation was "excellent" while more work was needed to bring economic cooperation to the same level.
